23	  examples/              # optional: test fixtures for local renders
24	    minimal.yaml
25	    full.yaml
26	```
27	
28	Rules:
29	
30	- The CLI selects a blueprint via positional argument:
31	  `intropy int create hello-world -o ./out`.
32	- Only `<blueprint>/template.yaml` is parsed; only `<blueprint>/skeleton/` is
33	  walked by the renderer.
34	- Anything else at the blueprint root (README, examples, CHANGELOG, ADRs) is
35	  invisible to the renderer — it's for the blueprint author, not the
36	  scaffolded project.
37	- There is **no shared content between blueprints**. No repo-level
38	  `skeletons/` dir, no cross-blueprint includes. If two blueprints need the
39	  same file, duplicate it.
40	
41	## Manifest schema (`<blueprint>/template.yaml`)
42	
43	```yaml
44	apiVersion: intropy.dev/v1
45	kind: Template
46	metadata:
47	  name: <kebab-case>           # convention: match the directory name
48	  title: <Title Case>
49	  description: <one sentence>
50	  tags: [example, go, http]
51	  labels:                      # free-form; no key is load-bearing today
52	    intropy.io/template-level: example
53	spec:
54	  parameters:                  # raw JSON Schema; type must be "object"
55	    type: object
56	    required: [name]
57	    properties:
58	      name:
59	        type: string
60	        title: Service name
61	        description: Lowercase kebab-case identifier.
62	        pattern: "^[a-z][a-z0-9-]*$"
63	      port:
64	        type: integer
65	        default: 8080
66	  values:                      # optional; derived values rendered via Go template + sprig
67	    module: 'github.com/example/{{ .name }}'
68	```
69	
70	Notes:
71	
72	- **`spec.parameters` is plain JSON Schema.** Types: `string`, `boolean`,
73	  `integer`, `number`. Supported attributes: `title`, `description`, `pattern`,
74	  `enum`, `default`. The same schema validates CLI inputs and drives the
75	  Backstage form when a Template entity references this blueprint.
76	- **Parameter declaration order matters** for human display. Keep the YAML
77	  order intentional.
78	- **`spec.values` derives string values from parameters.** Each entry is a Go
79	  template (with sprig) rendered against the resolved parameters. Use for
80	  composite values needed in multiple skeleton files (e.g. a module path).
81	  Output is always a string. Don't chain entries — map iteration order
82	  is non-deterministic.
83	- **No `spec.steps`**, no `spec.owner`, no `nextSteps`. The model is
84	  intentionally narrow: a manifest declares parameters and the skeleton tree
85	  describes what gets written.
86	
87	## Skeleton conventions (`<blueprint>/skeleton/`)
88	
89	- **File contents are templated only if the filename ends in `.tmpl`.** The
90	  `.tmpl` suffix is stripped on output (`README.md.tmpl` → `README.md`).
91	- **Filenames and directory names are templated** with the same `{{ .param }}`
92	  syntax as file contents (e.g. `src/{{ .name }}.csproj`). The `.tmpl` suffix
93	  only governs whether *file contents* are rendered; path segments are always
94	  templated.
95	- **Use `{{ .paramName }}` to reference parameters and derived values.** The
96	  data context is a flat map containing parameters + `spec.values` entries.
97	- **Sprig is available.** `upper`, `lower`, `title`, `kebabcase`,
98	  `snakecase`, `replace`, `default`, `trim`, `len`, `get`, `dict`. Full list:
99	  https://masterminds.github.io/sprig/ .
100	- **Missing keys are a hard error.** The renderer runs with
101	  `missingkey=error`. Typos like `{{ .Name }}` (wrong case) fail the render
102	  with a clear message — they don't silently produce empty strings.
103	- **Sprig functions with side effects exist** (`env`, `now`, `uuidv4`,
104	  `getHostByName`). Don't use them — they break the "same inputs → same
105	  output" reproducibility guarantee.
106	
107	Example skeleton file `skeleton/README.md.tmpl`:
108	
109	```markdown
110	# {{ .name }}
111	
112	Generated from the `{{ .name }}` blueprint.
113	
114	Module: `{{ .module }}`
115	```
116	
117	## The `AGENTS.md` convention
118	
119	Every skeleton ships an `AGENTS.md.tmpl` at its root. `AGENTS.md` (per the
120	[agents.md](https://agents.md/) standard, auto-loaded by most coding agents)
121	is the scaffolded project's **manifest for agents**: the facts about *this*
122	component that no skill can know. It is not a tutorial — generic framework
123	how-to lives in the Intropy skills collection (`intropy skills collection add
124	--name intropy --ref harbor.intropy.io/skills/index:latest`), which
125	`int create` offers to install into `.agents/skills/`.
126	
127	Each skeleton also ships a one-line `CLAUDE.md` containing exactly
128	`@AGENTS.md` — Claude Code doesn't auto-load AGENTS.md, so this import gives
129	it the same context. Keep it one line; never put content in it.
130	
131	Rules for authoring `AGENTS.md.tmpl`:
132	
133	- **Facts only, no teaching.** State what the component is, its component /
134	  topic / binding names (with rootPaths and ports), app id, and the key-file
135	  map. Do not restate framework conventions (naming-sync rules, builder
136	  usage, DI patterns) — those belong to the skills and duplicating them here
137	  drifts.
138	- **One canonical run path.** If the skeleton ships a `Taskfile.yml`,
139	  `task run` is canonical: `AGENTS.md` points at it and briefly says what it
140	  does; it never duplicates the underlying `dapr run` command. If there is no
141	  Taskfile, the raw `dapr run` command lives in `AGENTS.md` (and `README.md`
142	  must agree with it — same ports, same flags).
143	- **Project-specific deviations are facts.** Deliberate departures from
144	  framework defaults (e.g. "idempotency omitted in this sample; add
145	  `.WithIdempotency(...)` in …") belong in a short Development notes section.
146	- **One skills pointer.** End with a single "Framework guidance" line
147	  pointing at the skills collection — no per-skill routing table.
148	- **Section structure:** title + one-liner, Project overview, Important
149	  files, Build and run, optional Development notes / Testing, Framework
150	  guidance.
151	
152	The facts in `AGENTS.md` must match the skeleton (component YAML `metadata.name`
153	and rootPaths, `Constants.cs` values, Taskfile vars, `.http` ports). When you
154	change one, change the others in the same commit.
155	
156	## Adding a new blueprint
157	
158	1. Create the directory: `mkdir -p <name>/skeleton <name>/examples`.
159	2. Write `<name>/template.yaml` (manifest).
160	3. Write skeleton files under `<name>/skeleton/`. Suffix anything you want
161	   templated with `.tmpl`.
162	4. Write `<name>/README.md` describing what the blueprint produces and what
163	   parameters it takes (this is for humans browsing the repo, not for the
164	   scaffolded project).
165	5. Write at least one `<name>/examples/minimal.yaml` containing values that
166	   satisfy the required parameters.
167	6. Render it locally to confirm it works:
168	
169	   ```bash
170	   intropy int create <name> -o /tmp/<name>-out \
171	     -f <name>/examples/minimal.yaml --version main
172	   ```
173	
174	   Pass `--version main` while we don't have a release yet. Once releases
175	   exist, the default `--version` resolves to the latest tag.

3	description: >-
4	  Maintain `AGENTS.md` — the project-level manifest of an Intropy integration
5	  component (the terse agent-facing guide with package names, key files, run
6	  command, and ports) — plus the canonical project directory layout. Trigger
7	  when changing ports, the run command, or appId, when `AGENTS.md` is stale
8	  after a component change, or when deciding where a new file belongs.
9	  Trigger phrases: "update AGENTS.md", "change the app port", "the run command
10	  fails", "where does this file go". SKIP if editing Dapr component YAMLs
11	  under `local/dapr-components/` — that goes to `intropy-dapr`. SKIP if
12	  scaffolding a brand-new component — that goes to `intropy-getting-started`.

14	---
15	
16	# Intropy component manifest
17	
18	Every Intropy integration component carries a project-level manifest at its root: `AGENTS.md`, a terse project guide for agents working in the repo. It states the run command, ports, key files, and component names — the facts an agent needs before touching anything. This skill covers `AGENTS.md` plus the canonical directory layout it describes.
19	
20	## Project shape
21	
22	A scaffolded component looks like this:
23	
24	```
25	<component>/
26	├── AGENTS.md                     # agent-facing project guide (run command, ports, key files)
27	├── README.md
28	├── local/
29	│   └── dapr-components/         # local Dapr component YAMLs (pub/sub, bindings)
30	└── src/
31	    ├── Program.cs               # DI wiring + framework registration
32	    ├── <Component>.csproj
33	    ├── appsettings*.json
34	    ├── Configuration/
35	    │   └── Constants.cs         # component/topic/binding/customer names
36	    ├── Ingest/
37	    │   └── Endpoints.cs         # MapPost + .WithTopic + StepResult → response
38	    ├── Model/                   # in/out records
39	    └── Process/
40	        ├── <Entity>SendPipeline.cs            # implements ISendPipeline<Context>
41	        ├── <Entity>SendPipelineBuilder.cs     # fluent builder
42	        ├── ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs     # AddXxxSendPipeline()
43	        └── Steps/                             # one file per Block subclass
44	```
45	
46	Some blueprints add a `Taskfile.yml` (local-dev tasks wrapping the same run command) and `local/sample-data/`. When in doubt about where new code belongs, match this layout. Don't introduce parallel folders or rename existing ones — other tooling (and the scaffolder blueprint) rely on these paths.
47	
48	## `AGENTS.md` — the agent-facing project guide
49	
50	`AGENTS.md` is the project's manifest for agents: the facts about *this* component that no skill can know — what it is, its component/topic/binding names, ports, app id, key-file map, how to run it, and deliberate deviations from framework defaults. Keep it terse and concrete: bullet points, no prose essays.
51	
52	**Facts only — no teaching.** Don't restate generic framework conventions (naming-sync rules, builder usage, DI patterns) in `AGENTS.md`; they live in the skills and duplicated copies drift. Project-specific deviations (e.g. "idempotency deliberately omitted; add `.WithIdempotency(...)` in …") are facts and belong in a short Development notes section. End the file with a single "Framework guidance" pointer at the skills collection — no per-skill routing table.
53	
54	**The run command has one canonical home.** If the project ships a `Taskfile.yml`, `task run` is canonical: `AGENTS.md` points at it and says briefly what it does, never duplicating the underlying `dapr run` invocation. Without a Taskfile, the raw `dapr run` command lives in `AGENTS.md` (and `README.md` must agree — same ports, same flags). Wherever the command lives, what's load-bearing in it:
55	
56	- **`--app-id`** must match `Constants.ComponentName` (which is also what gets passed to `AddIntropyFramework(x => x.ComponentName = ...)`). It's the identity Dapr uses for the sidecar.
57	- **`--resources-path`** points at the directory of Dapr component YAMLs (`./local/dapr-components`). Keep it in sync with the actual on-disk path.
58	- **`--app-port`** (when the component has web endpoints) must match the `--urls` port in the `dotnet run` part of the command. If you change one, change the other.
59	
60	If you add a new Dapr component, you generally **don't** need to touch the run command — the sidecar discovers everything in the resources path. The component YAMLs themselves are covered by `intropy-dapr`.
61	
62	Update `AGENTS.md` whenever the facts it states change, so the next agent invocation has accurate context:
63	
64	- Added a state store, a binding, or a second pub/sub under `local/dapr-components/`.
65	- Renamed a topic or component (bump `Constants.cs` and the Dapr YAML in the same change).
66	- Changed the run command or ports.
67	
68	## What to avoid
69	
70	- **Don't let `--app-id` and `Constants.ComponentName` drift.** The mismatch is silent at compile time and shows up as Dapr identity confusion at runtime. Change both in the same commit.
71	- **Don't point `--resources-path` at a path that doesn't exist** — the sidecar starts with no components and messages disappear into the void.
72	- **Don't let `AGENTS.md` go stale.** A wrong run command or missing component listing misleads every future agent session in the repo. If the blueprint ships a `Taskfile.yml`, keep its vars in sync too.
73	- **Don't re-add cheat-sheet content.** If you're tempted to write a generic how-to bullet into `AGENTS.md` (how pub/sub works, how to wire a step), it belongs in a skill — `AGENTS.md` states only this project's facts.
74	- **Don't duplicate the run command.** One canonical home: `task run` when a `Taskfile.yml` exists, `AGENTS.md` otherwise. A second copy is a drift waiting to happen.
75	
76	## Verification
77	
78	- The canonical run command (`task run` when `Taskfile.yml` exists, otherwise the command in `AGENTS.md`) starts the component under Dapr — run it from the component root and confirm the app comes up on its app port and the sidecar loads the components from `local/dapr-components/`.
79	- Confirm the run command's `--app-id` matches `Constants.ComponentName` in `src/Configuration/Constants.cs`.
80	- Skim `AGENTS.md` and check that its run command, ports, and component listing match `Taskfile.yml` (if present) and `local/dapr-components/`.

18	---
19	
20	# Getting started with Intropy
21	
22	This skill covers exactly one journey: from nothing to a running Intropy integration component — first scaffold, first build, first message. If a project already exists, stop and use the feature-work skills instead (see the SKIP list in the description).
23	
24	An **Intropy blueprint** is a scaffold-style template: a manifest (`template.yaml`) declaring parameters, plus a skeleton file tree. The `intropy` CLI renders a blueprint plus your parameter values into a working project. Blueprints are fetched by release tag from the blueprint library, so the same inputs always produce the same output.
25	
26	## Prerequisites
27	
28	- **.NET 10 SDK** — the scaffolded projects are ASP.NET Core Minimal API / worker projects.
29	- **Dapr CLI, initialized** (`dapr init`) — components run under a Dapr sidecar locally.
30	- **The `intropy` CLI** — provides `intropy int create` (scaffolding) and `intropy skills add` (installs agent skills from `harbor.intropy.io/skills/<name>`).
31	
32	Install the CLI via Homebrew (macOS) or the install script (macOS / Linux; Windows via WSL 2):
33	
34	```bash
35	brew tap integrio-intropy/tap
36	brew trust --tap integrio-intropy/tap
37	brew install intropy
38	```
39	
40	```bash
41	curl -fsSL https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
42	```
43	
44	Verify the CLI is on your PATH before continuing:
45	
46	```bash
47	intropy --help
48	```
49	
50	## Available blueprints
51	
52	| Blueprint | What it scaffolds |
53	|---|---|
54	| `hello-world` | Minimal ASP.NET Minimal API with a Dapr pub/sub trigger and a transactional send pipeline. `POST /publish` publishes an order; a subscribed endpoint runs it through Deserialize → Validate → Transform → Serialize → Send. Best first project. |
55	| `transactional` | A .NET transactional integration job: polls a local inbound folder via a Dapr binding, publishes through in-memory pub/sub, runs a full VETER send pipeline, writes the transformed result to an outbound folder. Takes an extra `empty` boolean parameter — when `true`, pipeline step bodies throw `NotImplementedException` so an agent can fill them in. |
56	
57	Both blueprints take a required `name` parameter: a **PascalCase** identifier used for the .NET project, root namespace, and assembly. Dot-separated segments are allowed for nested namespaces (`MyApi`, `Int1055.OrderSync`). The blueprint derives a kebab-case `appId` from it for Dapr (e.g. `Int1055.OrderSync` → `int1055-ordersync`).
58	
59	## Scaffold
60	
61	1. Write a values file with the parameter values:
62	
63	   ```yaml
64	   # values.yaml
65	   name: HelloWorld
66	   ```
67	
68	2. Render the blueprint into an output directory:
69	
70	   ```bash
71	   intropy int create hello-world -o ./hello-world -f values.yaml
72	   ```
73	
74	Version selection:
75	
76	- No flag → the latest blueprint release.
77	- `--version v0.2.1` → that release tag.
78	- `--version main` → the default branch (useful before a release exists).
79	
80	Parameter values are validated against the blueprint's JSON Schema — a lowercase `name` fails the render with a pattern error rather than producing a broken project.
81	
82	## What you get
83	
84	A rendered `hello-world` project looks like this:
85	
86	```
87	hello-world/
88	├── AGENTS.md                     # agent-facing project guide (run command lives here)
89	├── README.md                    # human run instructions
90	├── local/
91	│   └── dapr-components/         # local Dapr component YAMLs
92	│       ├── pubsub.yaml          # in-memory pub/sub component
93	│       └── local-storage.yaml   # local file binding
94	└── src/
95	    ├── HelloWorld.csproj
96	    ├── HelloWorld.http          # sample requests for the first run
97	    ├── Program.cs               # DI wiring + framework + pipeline registration
98	    ├── appsettings*.json
99	    ├── Configuration/
100	    │   └── Constants.cs         # component/topic/binding names
101	    ├── Ingest/
102	    │   └── Endpoints.cs         # /publish + subscribed endpoint
103	    ├── Model/                   # OrderIn / OrderOut records
104	    └── Process/
105	        ├── OrderSendPipeline.cs
106	        ├── OrderSendPipelineBuilder.cs
107	        ├── ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs
108	        └── Steps/               # one file per pipeline step
109	```
110	
111	The `transactional` blueprint follows the same shape and additionally ships a `Taskfile.yml` with local-dev tasks and `local/sample-data/` with a sample order that `task run` seeds into the inbound folder.
112	
113	The rendered `README.md` and `AGENTS.md` are per-project and authoritative — they carry the exact run command with the right `appId` and ports for what you scaffolded.
114	
115	## First run
116	
117	From the project root:
118	
119	1. **Build:**
120	
121	   ```bash
122	   dotnet build ./src
123	   ```
124	
125	2. **Run under Dapr.** When the blueprint ships a `Taskfile.yml`, `task run` is the canonical run path; otherwise use the run command from the project's `AGENTS.md`. For `hello-world` (no Taskfile) it is:
126	
127	   ```bash
128	   dapr run \
129	     --app-id hello-world \
130	     --app-port 5001 \
131	     --dapr-http-port 3500 \
132	     --resources-path ./local/dapr-components \
133	     -- dotnet run --project ./src --urls http://localhost:5001
134	   ```
135	
136	3. **Publish a sample message.** Open `src/<Name>.http` and send the `POST /publish` request (from an editor with .http support, or copy it into curl):
137	
138	   ```http
139	   POST http://localhost:5001/publish
140	   Content-Type: application/json
141	
142	   {
143	     "orderId": "ORD-1001",
144	     "customerId": "CUST-42",
145	     "amount": 39.90
146	   }
147	   ```
148	
149	   Dapr delivers the published message to the subscribed endpoint, which runs it through the send pipeline. The `.http` file also has a `GET /dapr/subscribe` request to inspect the discovered subscriptions.
150	
151	For `transactional`, the first run is file-driven and Taskfile-managed: `task run` seeds the inbound folder with `local/sample-data/sample-order.json`, starts the local observability stack, and runs the job once under Dapr; the job picks the file up, processes it, and writes the transformed JSON to the outbound folder.
152

Every Intropy integration component carries a project-level manifest at its root: `AGENTS.md`, a terse project guide for agents working in the repo. It states the run command, ports, key files, and component names — the facts an agent needs before touching anything. This skill covers `AGENTS.md` plus the canonical directory layout it describes.

## Project shape

A scaffolded component looks like this:

```
<component>/
├── AGENTS.md                     # agent-facing project guide (run command, ports, key files)
├── README.md
├── local/
│   └── dapr-components/         # local Dapr component YAMLs (pub/sub, bindings)
└── src/
    ├── Program.cs               # DI wiring + framework registration
    ├── <Component>.csproj
    ├── appsettings*.json
    ├── Configuration/
    │   └── Constants.cs         # component/topic/binding/customer names
    ├── Ingest/
    │   └── Endpoints.cs         # MapPost + .WithTopic + StepResult → response
    ├── Model/                   # in/out records
    └── Process/
        ├── <Entity>SendPipeline.cs            # implements ISendPipeline<Context>
        ├── <Entity>SendPipelineBuilder.cs     # fluent builder
        ├── ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs     # AddXxxSendPipeline()
        └── Steps/                             # one file per Block subclass
```

Some blueprints add a `Taskfile.yml` (local-dev tasks wrapping the same run command) and `local/sample-data/`. When in doubt about where new code belongs, match this layout. Don't introduce parallel folders or rename existing ones — other tooling (and the scaffolder blueprint) rely on these paths.

## `AGENTS.md` — the agent-facing project guide

`AGENTS.md` is the project's manifest for agents: the facts about *this* component that no skill can know — what it is, its component/topic/binding names, ports, app id, key-file map, how to run it, and deliberate deviations from framework defaults. Keep it terse and concrete: bullet points, no prose essays.

**Facts only — no teaching.** Don't restate generic framework conventions (naming-sync rules, builder usage, DI patterns) in `AGENTS.md`; they live in the skills and duplicated copies drift. Project-specific deviations (e.g. "idempotency deliberately omitted; add `.WithIdempotency(...)` in …") are facts and belong in a short Development notes section. End the file with a single "Framework guidance" pointer at the skills collection — no per-skill routing table.

**The run command has one canonical home.** If the project ships a `Taskfile.yml`, `task run` is canonical: `AGENTS.md` points at it and says briefly what it does, never duplicating the underlying `dapr run` invocation. Without a Taskfile, the raw `dapr run` command lives in `AGENTS.md` (and `README.md` must agree — same ports, same flags). Wherever the command lives, what's load-bearing in it:

- **`--app-id`** must match `Constants.ComponentName` (which is also what gets passed to `AddIntropyFramework(x => x.ComponentName = ...)`). It's the identity Dapr uses for the sidecar.
- **`--resources-path`** points at the directory of Dapr component YAMLs (`./local/dapr-components`). Keep it in sync with the actual on-disk path.
- **`--app-port`** (when the component has web endpoints) must match the `--urls` port in the `dotnet run` part of the command. If you change one, change the other.

If you add a new Dapr component, you generally **don't** need to touch the run command — the sidecar discovers everything in the resources path. The component YAMLs themselves are covered by `intropy-dapr`.

Update `AGENTS.md` whenever the facts it states change, so the next agent invocation has accurate context:

- Added a state store, a binding, or a second pub/sub under `local/dapr-components/`.
- Renamed a topic or component (bump `Constants.cs` and the Dapr YAML in the same change).
- Changed the run command or ports.

## What to avoid

- **Don't let `--app-id` and `Constants.ComponentName` drift.** The mismatch is silent at compile time and shows up as Dapr identity confusion at runtime. Change both in the same commit.
- **Don't point `--resources-path` at a path that doesn't exist** — the sidecar starts with no components and messages disappear into the void.
- **Don't let `AGENTS.md` go stale.** A wrong run command or missing component listing misleads every future agent session in the repo. If the blueprint ships a `Taskfile.yml`, keep its vars in sync too.
- **Don't re-add cheat-sheet content.** If you're tempted to write a generic how-to bullet into `AGENTS.md` (how pub/sub works, how to wire a step), it belongs in a skill — `AGENTS.md` states only this project's facts.
- **Don't duplicate the run command.** One canonical home: `task run` when a `Taskfile.yml` exists, `AGENTS.md` otherwise. A second copy is a drift waiting to happen.

## Verification

- The canonical run command (`task run` when `Taskfile.yml` exists, otherwise the command in `AGENTS.md`) starts the component under Dapr — run it from the component root and confirm the app comes up on its app port and the sidecar loads the components from `local/dapr-components/`.

- Skim `AGENTS.md` and check that its run command, ports, and component listing match `Taskfile.yml` (if present) and `local/dapr-components/`.

# Getting started with Intropy

This skill covers exactly one journey: from nothing to a running Intropy integration component — first scaffold, first build, first message. If a project already exists, stop and use the feature-work skills instead (see the SKIP list in the description).

An **Intropy blueprint** is a scaffold-style template: a manifest (`template.yaml`) declaring parameters, plus a skeleton file tree. The `intropy` CLI renders a blueprint plus your parameter values into a working project. Blueprints are fetched by release tag from the blueprint library, so the same inputs always produce the same output.

## Prerequisites

- **.NET 10 SDK** — the scaffolded projects are ASP.NET Core Minimal API / worker projects.
- **Dapr CLI, initialized** (`dapr init`) — components run under a Dapr sidecar locally.
- **The `intropy` CLI** — provides `intropy int create` (scaffolding) and `intropy skills add` (installs agent skills from `harbor.intropy.io/skills/<name>`).

Install the CLI via Homebrew (macOS) or the install script (macOS / Linux; Windows via WSL 2):

```bash
brew tap integrio-intropy/tap
brew trust --tap integrio-intropy/tap
brew install intropy
```

```bash
curl -fsSL https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
```

Verify the CLI is on your PATH before continuing:

```bash
intropy --help
```

## Available blueprints

| Blueprint | What it scaffolds |
|---|---|
| `hello-world` | Minimal ASP.NET Minimal API with a Dapr pub/sub trigger and a transactional send pipeline. `POST /publish` publishes an order; a subscribed endpoint runs it through Deserialize → Validate → Transform → Serialize → Send. Best first project. |
| `transactional` | A .NET transactional integration job: polls a local inbound folder via a Dapr binding, publishes through in-memory pub/sub, runs a full VETER send pipeline, writes the transformed result to an outbound folder. Takes an extra `empty` boolean parameter — when `true`, pipeline step bodies throw `NotImplementedException` so an agent can fill them in. |

Both blueprints take a required `name` parameter: a **PascalCase** identifier used for the .NET project, root namespace, and assembly. Dot-separated segments are allowed for nested namespaces (`MyApi`, `Int1055.OrderSync`). The blueprint derives a kebab-case `appId` from it for Dapr (e.g. `Int1055.OrderSync` → `int1055-ordersync`).

## Scaffold

1. Write a values file with the parameter values:

   ```yaml
   # values.yaml
   name: HelloWorld
   ```

2. Render the blueprint into an output directory:

   ```bash
   intropy int create hello-world -o ./hello-world -f values.yaml
   ```

Version selection:

- No flag → the latest blueprint release.
- `--version v0.2.1` → that release tag.
- `--version main` → the default branch (useful before a release exists).

Parameter values are validated against the blueprint's JSON Schema — a lowercase `name` fails the render with a pattern error rather than producing a broken project.

## What you get

A rendered `hello-world` project looks like this:

```
hello-world/
├── AGENTS.md                     # agent-facing project guide (run command lives here)
├── README.md                    # human run instructions
├── local/
│   └── dapr-components/         # local Dapr component YAMLs
│       ├── pubsub.yaml          # in-memory pub/sub component
│       └── local-storage.yaml   # local file binding
└── src/
    ├── HelloWorld.csproj
    ├── HelloWorld.http          # sample requests for the first run
    ├── Program.cs               # DI wiring + framework + pipeline registration
    ├── appsettings*.json
    ├── Configuration/
    │   └── Constants.cs         # component/topic/binding names
    ├── Ingest/
    │   └── Endpoints.cs         # /publish + subscribed endpoint
    ├── Model/                   # OrderIn / OrderOut records
    └── Process/
        ├── OrderSendPipeline.cs
        ├── OrderSendPipelineBuilder.cs
        ├── ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs
        └── Steps/               # one file per pipeline step
```

The `transactional` blueprint follows the same shape and additionally ships a `Taskfile.yml` with local-dev tasks and `local/sample-data/` with a sample order that `task run` seeds into the inbound folder.

The rendered `README.md` and `AGENTS.md` are per-project and authoritative — they carry the exact run command with the right `appId` and ports for what you scaffolded.

## First run

From the project root:

1. **Build:**

   ```bash
   dotnet build ./src
   ```

2. **Run under Dapr.** When the blueprint ships a `Taskfile.yml`, `task run` is the canonical run path; otherwise use the run command from the project's `AGENTS.md`. For `hello-world` (no Taskfile) it is:

   ```bash
   dapr run \
     --app-id hello-world \
     --app-port 5001 \
     --dapr-http-port 3500 \
     --resources-path ./local/dapr-components \
     -- dotnet run --project ./src --urls http://localhost:5001
   ```

3. **Publish a sample message.** Open `src/<Name>.http` and send the `POST /publish` request (from an editor with .http support, or copy it into curl):

   ```http
   POST http://localhost:5001/publish
   Content-Type: application/json

   {
     "orderId": "ORD-1001",
     "customerId": "CUST-42",
     "amount": 39.90
   }
   ```

   Dapr delivers the published message to the subscribed endpoint, which runs it through the send pipeline. The `.http` file also has a `GET /dapr/subscribe` request to inspect the discovered subscriptions.

For `transactional`, the first run is file-driven and Taskfile-managed: `task run` seeds the inbound folder with `local/sample-data/sample-order.json`, starts the local observability stack, and runs the job once under Dapr; the job picks the file up, processes it, and writes the transformed JSON to the outbound folder.

## Where to go next

Once the component runs, this skill's job is done. Feature work — new pipeline steps, enrichment lookups, endpoints, Dapr components, manifest changes — is covered by the sibling skills: `intropy-pipeline`, `intropy-blocks`, `intropy-endpoint`, `intropy-dapr`, and `intropy-manifest`.

## Verification

- Inspect the rendered output directory: the tree matches the project shape above, and `{{ .name }}` placeholders are fully resolved (project file is `src/<Name>.csproj`, no `.tmpl` suffixes remain).
- `dotnet build ./src` succeeds from the project root.
- The canonical run command (`task run`, or the `dapr run` command from `AGENTS.md` when there is no Taskfile) starts the app and the sidecar; sending the `POST /publish` request from `src/<Name>.http` returns 200 and the logs show the subscribed endpoint receiving the message and the pipeline completing (for `transactional`: the transformed `<orderId>.json` appears in the outbound folder).

Base directory for this skill: /Users/robinhultman/.claude/skills/intropy-docs

# Intropy Documentation

The shared foundation for writing any Intropy documentation in Backstage TechDocs.

This skill covers writing conventions, TechDocs structure, Intropy domain model
terminology, and templates for every type of documentation page in the Intropy
ecosystem. Whether you're writing a block reference page, a blueprint pattern spec,
an archetype overview, or a setup guide — start here.

## When NOT to use this skill

For per-blueprint golden path tutorials that walk developers through scaffolded
Backstage template code (explaining TODOs, file-by-file walkthroughs), use the
**blueprint-golden-path** skill instead. This skill covers the WHAT and WHY;
blueprint-golden-path covers the HOW step-by-step.

## What this skill covers

| Documentation type | Template | When to use |
|-------------------|----------|-------------|
| **Block reference page** | `references/block-template.md` | Documenting what a generic block type IS (Extractor, Loader, etc.) |
| **Blueprint pattern page** | `references/blueprint-template.md` | Documenting a named composition as a reusable pattern (Golden Record, etc.) |
| **Archetype page** | `references/archetype-template.md` | Documenting an abstract behavioural model (Pub/Sub, Aggregator, API Service) |
| **Connector concept page** | `references/connector-reference.md` | Explaining what Connectors are and how they relate to Blocks |
| **Pattern reference catalog** | Use `scripts/scaffold.py` | Generating the complete catalog with all blocks, blueprints, archetypes |
| **Environment setup guide** | No template — follow writing principles | Common onboarding: tools, access, prerequisites |
| **Architecture overview** | `references/architecture-overview-template.md` | High-level explanation of how Intropy works |

## Workflow

### 1. Understand what you're writing

Determine which type of documentation the user needs. If they say "document the
Extractor", that's a block reference page. If they say "write up the Golden Record
pattern", that's a blueprint pattern page. If they're unclear, ask.

For the **full pattern reference catalog** (all blocks + blueprints + archetypes),
use the scaffold script:

```bash
python scripts/scaffold.py --type catalog --output-dir ./output
```

### 2. Read the relevant references

**Always read first:**
- `references/intropy-model.md` — The authoritative domain model. Read this to use
  terminology correctly. Blocks, Blueprints, Connectors, Systems, Integrations,
  and Archetypes all have precise meanings.

**Then read the relevant template:**
- Block page → `references/block-template.md`
- Blueprint page → `references/blueprint-template.md`
- Archetype page → `references/archetype-template.md`
- Connector explanation → `references/connector-reference.md`
- Architecture overview → `references/architecture-overview-template.md`

**For TechDocs structure and MkDocs configuration:**
- `references/techdocs-structure.md` — File layout, mkdocs.yml patterns, catalog-info.yaml

### 3. Write using Intropy conventions

These principles apply to ALL Intropy documentation, regardless of type.

**Use terminology precisely.** The Intropy model has specific terms with specific
meanings. A Connector is not a "plugin" — it's accumulated organizational knowledge
about an external system. A Blueprint is not a "template" — it's a named composition
of Block types. Read `references/intropy-model.md` if unsure.

**Describe the invariant, not the variant.** When writing about generic patterns
(blocks, blueprints, archetypes), every sentence should be true for ALL instances.
"An Extractor pulls data from a source system" — not "An Extractor pulls data from
Dynamics." Specific systems belong in golden path tutorials, not reference pages.

**Define responsibility boundaries clearly.** The most important thing about a block
or blueprint doc is where responsibilities start and stop. An Extractor handles
source system communication but does NOT transform data into the internal model.
These boundaries are what make blocks composable.

**Explain the failure model.** Edge blocks handle business errors (expected operational
conditions). Core blocks treat bad input as bugs (unexpected). This distinction is
fundamental. Make it prominent and concrete with generic examples.

**Show the Connector contract.** For edge blocks, the Connector interface is what
makes them reusable across systems. Document the generic interface — what any
Connector must provide — so Connector developers know what to implement.

**Use TechDocs admonitions.** Use MkDocs admonition syntax for callouts:

```markdown
!!! info "Why does this matter?"
    Explanation of architectural reasoning.

!!! warning "Common mistake"
    What goes wrong and how to avoid it.

!!! note "Prerequisites"
    What the reader needs before continuing.
```

**Cross-reference generously.** Every block page should link to its archetype page
and the blueprints it appears in. Every blueprint page should link to its block
pages. Every archetype page should link to the blocks that follow it. This
bidirectional linking reinforces the conceptual framework.

### 4. Structure for TechDocs

Read `references/techdocs-structure.md` for the full details. The essentials:

- **techdocs-core** is the only allowed MkDocs plugin
- **nav is required** — TechDocs uses it for the sidebar
- Use `assets/mkdocs-template.yml` as the base configuration
- File naming: lowercase, hyphenated (e.g., `transactional-integration.md`)
- Every TechDocs site needs a `catalog-info.yaml` for Backstage registration

### 5. Deliver the output

Save the complete documentation to the output directory. For a full catalog,
the deliverable is:

```
intropy-pattern-reference/
├── mkdocs.yml
├── catalog-info.yaml
└── docs/
    ├── index.md
    ├── connectors.md
    ├── archetypes/
    │   ├── pubsub.md
    │   ├── aggregator.md
    │   └── api-service.md
    ├── blocks/
    │   ├── extractor.md
    │   ├── loader.md
    │   ├── reconciler.md
    │   ├── assembler.md
    │   └── transactional-integration.md
    └── blueprints/
        ├── golden-record.md
        ├── product-sync.md
        └── order-import.md
```

For individual pages, deliver the markdown file ready to drop into an existing
TechDocs site.

## Relationship to blueprint-golden-path

This skill produces **reference documentation** — what things ARE, how they work,
when to use them. The `blueprint-golden-path` skill produces **tutorials** — step-by-step
guides that walk developers through scaffolded template code for a specific blueprint.

The reference docs from this skill serve as context for golden path tutorials. When
the blueprint-golden-path skill writes a tutorial for the Golden Record blueprint,
it reads the block and blueprint reference pages produced by this skill to understand
the architectural context.

Think of it as: this skill writes the **"what and why"**, blueprint-golden-path
writes the **"how, step by step"**.

## Reference files

Read these as needed during documentation work:

- `references/intropy-model.md` — Complete Intropy domain model (Blocks, Blueprints, Connectors, Archetypes)
- `references/techdocs-structure.md` — TechDocs file layout, mkdocs.yml patterns, Backstage integration
- `references/writing-guide.md` — Writing style, tone, and structural patterns for all doc types
- `references/block-template.md` — Template for generic block type reference pages
- `references/blueprint-template.md` — Template for generic blueprint pattern pages
- `references/archetype-template.md` — Template for archetype pages
- `references/connector-reference.md` — Connector concept reference (what Connectors are)
- `references/architecture-overview-template.md` — Template for the Intropy architecture overview page

1	# Working with AI assistants
2	
3	Intropy ships **agent skills** for AI coding assistants like Claude Code. Each skill teaches the assistant one Intropy capability: the conventions, the load-bearing rules, and how to verify a change. Instead of rediscovering the house style every session, the assistant follows the same playbook an Intropy maintainer would.
4	
5	## What Intropy gives an AI assistant
6	
7	An AI assistant is only as good as the structure it works within. A plain .NET repo leaves the big decisions open: which abstraction owns which responsibility, where the wiring goes, what shape a new piece of code should take. An assistant fills those gaps by guessing, and every guess is a chance for the result to drift away from how your team builds.
8	
9	Intropy's structure removes the guesswork. Blocks have a known surface. Blueprints compose them in a documented order. Every scaffolded project carries an `agent.md`, a terse agent-facing guide to the project layout and run command. Together these act as guardrails: instead of inventing a design, the assistant works within one, and the skills codify which convention applies when.
10	
11	The catalogue is deliberately fine-grained: one capability per skill. Each skill's description carries the trigger situations it covers and explicit redirects to its siblings, so the assistant loads exactly the guidance the task needs. Ask it to write a step class and it gets the Block conventions; ask it to wire that step into the pipeline and it gets the composition rules instead.
12	
13	## Enable AI assistance in your project
14	
15	Skills are published as OCI artifacts and managed with the `intropy` CLI.

# Working with AI assistants

Intropy ships **agent skills** for AI coding assistants like Claude Code. Each skill teaches the assistant one Intropy capability: the conventions, the load-bearing rules, and how to verify a change. Instead of rediscovering the house style every session, the assistant follows the same playbook an Intropy maintainer would.

## What Intropy gives an AI assistant

An AI assistant is only as good as the structure it works within. A plain .NET repo leaves the big decisions open: which abstraction owns which responsibility, where the wiring goes, what shape a new piece of code should take. An assistant fills those gaps by guessing, and every guess is a chance for the result to drift away from how your team builds.

Intropy's structure removes the guesswork. Blocks have a known surface. Blueprints compose them in a documented order. Every scaffolded project carries an `agent.md`, a terse agent-facing guide to the project layout and run command. Together these act as guardrails: instead of inventing a design, the assistant works within one, and the skills codify which convention applies when.

The catalogue is deliberately fine-grained: one capability per skill. Each skill's description carries the trigger situations it covers and explicit redirects to its siblings, so the assistant loads exactly the guidance the task needs. Ask it to write a step class and it gets the Block conventions; ask it to wire that step into the pipeline and it gets the composition rules instead.

## Enable AI assistance in your project

Skills are published as OCI artifacts and managed with the `intropy` CLI.

!!! note "Prerequisites"
    The [Intropy CLI](../reference/cli/index.md) is on your `PATH` (`intropy --help` prints the verbs), and your AI coding assistant loads `SKILL.md`-format skills. Claude Code is the reference implementation; any assistant that reads the same skill format works.

**New integrations get skills at scaffold time.** After rendering a Blueprint, `intropy int create` offers to install the Intropy skill collection into the new project (`[Y/n]`, default yes):

```
$ intropy int create hello-world -n OrderSync
created OrderSync from integrio-intropy/intropy-blueprints (blueprint hello-world)
Install agent skills into .agents/skills? [Y/n]:
  installed intropy-pipeline @ 0.1.1 -> .agents/skills/intropy-pipeline
  ...
installed 9 skill(s) from harbor.intropy.io/skills/index:latest
```

In non-interactive runs (CI, the Backstage scaffolder) the prompt is skipped; pass `--install-skills` to install without prompting, or `--skip-install-skills` to opt out silently.

**Existing projects register the collection once** — this caches the catalogue index so skills can be installed by name:

```bash
intropy skills collection add --name intropy --ref harbor.intropy.io/skills/index:latest
intropy skills add --name intropy-getting-started
```

Either way, skills land in the project's `.agents/skills/` directory, and the CLI records them in two files at the project root: `skills.json` (what's registered and installed) and `skills.lock.json` (exact digests and install paths). Commit both — that's what makes the skill set travel with the repo, so teammates and CI agents that open the project get identical skills. To pin an exact version, install by full OCI reference instead of by name:

```bash
intropy skills add harbor.intropy.io/skills/intropy-pipeline:0.1.1
```

When the catalogue publishes a new version, refresh the cached index and reconcile:

```bash
intropy skills collection update intropy
intropy skills update --all
```

## The skill catalogue

### Building an integration

| Skill | What it covers |
|---|---|
| `intropy-getting-started` | Bootstrap a new integration from a Blueprint with `intropy int create`, then the first build and run under Dapr with a sample message. |
| `intropy-pipeline` | Compose the transactional send pipeline: step order, the builder, and DI wiring. |
| `intropy-blocks` | Author Block step classes, including the choice between `BusinessStepResult` and `TechnicalStepResult` that decides retry-versus-drop behaviour. |
| `intropy-endpoint` | HTTP and subscribe endpoints, and the canonical mapping from step results to responses and pub/sub ack semantics. |
| `intropy-dapr` | Dapr components: pub/sub, bindings, state stores, and keeping component names in sync between code and YAML. |
| `intropy-manifest` | The `agent.md` project guide and the canonical project layout. |
| `intropy-testing` | xUnit tests for individual Block steps and for composed pipelines run in-process. |
| `intropy-code-review` | Review an integration component against Intropy conventions: pipeline shape, result-type choices, naming drift. |

### Authoring Blueprints

| Skill | What it covers |
|---|---|
| `intropy-blueprint-authoring` | Author the Blueprints themselves: `template.yaml` manifests, skeleton trees, and local render verification. |

More skills are on the roadmap and will appear in the collection as they ship — run `intropy skills collection update intropy` to pick them up: choosing a golden path (`intropy-architecture`), building and consuming Connectors (`intropy-connector`), and migrating BizTalk or Logic Apps integrations (`intropy-migrate`).

### In practice

A normal session looks like one of three shapes.

**Starting from nothing.** With `intropy-getting-started` installed, prompt:

> Scaffold a new Intropy integration called OrderSync and run it with a sample message.

The assistant writes a values file, renders the Blueprint with `intropy int create`, and takes the project through its first build and run under a Dapr sidecar. The scaffold step installs the full skill collection into the new project along the way, so by the time the first message flows through the pipeline, the assistant is already equipped for the feature work that follows.

**Feature work in an existing component.** Prompt:

> Add a Validate step to the OrderSendPipeline that rejects orders without a customer number.

Two skills cooperate: `intropy-blocks` shapes the step class and picks the result type (a rejected order is a business outcome, not a technical failure, and the distinction decides whether the message is dropped or retried), while `intropy-pipeline` places the step in the chain and wires it into DI. You review the diff before committing.

**Reviewing a change.** Prompt:

> Review this component. Is the pipeline idiomatic Intropy?

`intropy-code-review` works through the convention checklists: step ordering, result-type choices, naming sync between code and Dapr YAML, and manifest drift, reporting findings most severe first.

Every skill ends with a verification section, so the assistant doesn't just make the change: it builds, runs, and checks the expected output before reporting done.

## Machine-readable docs

This documentation site is also exposed in a form built for AI consumption. Point your assistant at:

- `https://docs.intropy.example/llms.txt` — a structured index of canonical pages, following the [llmstxt.org](https://llmstxt.org/) convention.

The `llms.txt` file is the right input when an assistant needs the docs but shouldn't ingest the full site. It enumerates Concepts, References, How-tos, and Tutorials with one-line descriptions so the assistant can fetch the page that actually answers the question.

## What's next

- [Quick start](quick-start.md) — scaffold and run your first integration by hand
- [Migrate to Intropy with AI assistance](../migration/with-ai-assistance.md) — the AI-assisted migration loop for BizTalk solutions
- [`intropy` CLI reference](../reference/cli/index.md) — the commands the skills wrap

| `intropy-endpoint` | HTTP and subscribe endpoints, and the canonical mapping from step results to responses and pub/sub ack semantics. |
| `intropy-dapr` | Dapr components: pub/sub, bindings, state stores, and keeping component names in sync between code and YAML. |
| `intropy-manifest` | The `agent.md` project guide and the canonical project layout. |
| `intropy-testing` | xUnit tests for individual Block steps and for composed pipelines run in-process. |
| `intropy-code-review` | Review an integration component against Intropy conventions: pipeline shape, result-type choices, naming drift. |

### Authoring Blueprints

| Skill | What it covers |
|---|---|
| `intropy-blueprint-authoring` | Author the Blueprints themselves: `template.yaml` manifests, skeleton trees, and local render verification. |

More skills are on the roadmap and will appear in the collection as they ship — run `intropy skills collection update intropy` to pick them up: choosing a golden path (`intropy-architecture`), building and consuming Connectors (`intropy-connector`), and migrating BizTalk or Logic Apps integrations (`intropy-migrate`).

### In practice

A normal session looks like one of three shapes.

**Starting from nothing.** With `intropy-getting-started` installed, prompt:

> Scaffold a new Intropy integration called OrderSync and run it with a sample message.

The assistant writes a values file, renders the Blueprint with `intropy int create`, and takes the project through its first build and run under a Dapr sidecar. The scaffold step installs the full skill collection into the new project along the way, so by the time the first message flows through the pipeline, the assistant is already equipped for the feature work that follows.

**Feature work in an existing component.** Prompt:

> Add a Validate step to the OrderSendPipeline that rejects orders without a customer number.

Two skills cooperate: `intropy-blocks` shapes the step class and picks the result type (a rejected order is a business outcome, not a technical failure, and the distinction decides whether the message is dropped or retried), while `intropy-pipeline` places the step in the chain and wires it into DI. You review the diff before committing.

**Reviewing a change.** Prompt:

> Review this component. Is the pipeline idiomatic Intropy?

`intropy-code-review` works through the convention checklists: step ordering, result-type choices, naming sync between code and Dapr YAML, and manifest drift, reporting findings most severe first.

Every skill ends with a verification section, so the assistant doesn't just make the change: it builds, runs, and checks the expected output before reporting done.

./local/test/out/)]:::ext 29 30 dev -->|OrderIn| pub 31 bind --> file 32 33 classDef block fill:#1e1a2e,stroke:#8066FF,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#e6e1f5; 34 classDef ext fill:#0f0d1a,stroke:#21EAC7,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#cfeee6; 35 classDef dapr fill:#141225,stroke:#8066FF,stroke-width:1.5px,stroke-dasharray:4 3,color:#c8bfe8; 36 ``` 37 38 In the diagram: your code is Lilac, external touchpoints are Peppermint, and Dapr's plumbing is dashed. 39 40 ## Before you begin 41 42 - The [CLI is installed](install.md) — along with .NET 10 SDK, Docker Desktop 27+, and Dapr CLI 1.16 43 - A scratch directory you don't mind throwing away 44 45 ## Steps 46 47 ### 1. Scaffold the integration 48 49 ```bash 50 intropy int create hello-world -n HelloWorld 51 ``` 52 53 [`intropy int create`](../reference/cli/create.md) scaffolds an ASP.NET Minimal API project targeting .NET 10, wired with Dapr pub/sub and a transactional send pipeline built from Intropy framework Blocks. The positional `hello-world` picks which blueprint to render; `-n` names the integration and, with `-o` omitted, becomes the output directory the CLI creates. 54 55 ### 2. Inspect what was generated 56 57 ``` 58 HelloWorld/ 59 ├── .gitignore 60 ├── agent.md # guidance for AI assistants working in this project 61 ├── README.md 62 ├── local/ 63 │ └── dapr-components/ 64 │ ├── pubsub.yaml # in-memory pub/sub for local runs 65 │ └── local-storage.yaml # local file binding 66 └── src/ 67 ├── HelloWorld.csproj # net10.0, Dapr.AspNetCore, Intropy.Libs.Framework 68 ├── HelloWorld.http # sample HTTP requests 69 ├── appsettings.json # + appsettings.Development.json 70 ├── Program.cs # host + DI + pipeline wiring 71 ├── Properties/launchSettings.json # dotnet run profiles 72 ├── Configuration/Constants.cs # component/topic/binding names 73 ├── Ingest/Endpoints.cs # POST /publish and POST /subscribe 74 ├── Model/ # OrderIn, OrderOut DTOs 75 └── Process/ 76 ├── OrderSendPipeline.cs 77 ├── OrderSendPipelineBuilder.cs 78 ├── ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs 79 └── Steps/ # Deserialize → Validate → Transform → Serialize → Send 80 ``` 81 82 The scaffold is a complete, runnable Integration — not a stub. It publishes an `OrderIn` payload to a Dapr pub/sub topic, then subscribes to that same topic and runs each message through a five-step send pipeline. 83 84 ### 3. Read the pipeline wiring 85 86 `Program.cs` is a standard ASP.NET Minimal API host. The Intropy-specific part is the **send pipeline** — five Blocks composed in order: 87 88 ```csharp title="Program.cs (excerpt)" 89 builder.Services.AddDaprClient(); 90 91 builder.Services.AddIntropyFramework(x => 92 { 93 x.ComponentName = Constants.ComponentName; 94 x.ServiceNamespace = Constants.CustomerName; 95 }); 96 97 builder.Services.AddOrderSendPipeline((pipelineBuilder, sp) => pipelineBuilder 98 .WithDeserializer(new OrderDeserializeStep()) 99 .WithValidator(new OrderValidateStep()) 100 .WithTransformer(new OrderTransformStep()) 101 .WithSerializer(new OrderSerializeStep()) 102 .WithSender(new OrderSendStep(sp.GetRequiredService()))); 103 ``` 104 105 This send pipeline defines the following steps: Deserialize → Validate → Transform → Serialize → Send. Each step has its own file under `src/Process/Steps/` so it's unit-testable in isolation. 106 107 The two endpoints in `src/Ingest/Endpoints.cs` close the loop: 108 109 - `POST /publish` — the **trigger**: the public route you call to start the integration. Accepts an `OrderIn` and publishes it to the `pubsub` component on topic `messages` 110 - `POST /subscribe` — not a route you call; the internal handler Dapr invokes off the queue, pulling each message through the send pipeline 111 112 ### 4. Run it 113 114 From inside `HelloWorld/`, launch the app with its Dapr sidecar: 115 116 ```bash 117 cd HelloWorld 118 dapr run \ 119 --app-id hello-world \ 120 --app-port 5001 \ 121 --dapr-http-port 3500 \ 122 --resources-path ./local/dapr-components \ 123 -- dotnet run --project ./src --urls http://localhost:5001 124 ``` 125 126 Once you see `dapr application discovered`, send a sample order from another terminal: 127 128 ```bash 129 curl -X POST http://localhost:5001/publish \ 130 -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ 131 -d '{ 132 "orderId": "ORD-1001", 133 "customerId": "CUST-42", 134 "amount": 39.90 135 }' 136 ``` 137 138 `POST /publish` returns `202 Accepted`. Dapr then delivers the message to `POST /subscribe`, which pulls it through the send pipeline. If your editor supports `.http` files, `src/HelloWorld.http` sends the same request. 139 140 ### 5. Inspect the result 141 142 The Sender step writes each processed order as a JSON file through the `local-storage` Dapr binding. The binding's `rootPath` (see `local/dapr-components/local-storage.yaml`) is `./local/test/out`, relative to the directory you launched the app from: 143 144 ```bash 145 ls ./local/test/out 146 ``` 147 148 Read the file: 149 150 ```bash 151 cat ./local/test/out/order-*.json 152 ``` 153 154 ```json 155 { 156 "OrderId": "ORD-1001", 157 "CustomerId": "CUST-42", 158 "ProcessedAt": "2026-05-17T09:42:13.1234567+00:00", 159 "Amount": 39.90, 160 "Status": "Processed" 161 } 162 ``` 163 164 That's the output of the full pipeline: the inbound `OrderIn` was validated, transformed into an `OrderOut` — stamped with a `ProcessedAt` timestamp and `Status: "Processed"` — serialized, and written through the Dapr binding. Re-run the curl from step 4 to see another file appear. 165 166 ## What's next 167 168 - [The Intropy model](../concepts/intropy-model.md) — read this before going further 169 - [Build a point-to-point integration](../tutorials/point-to-point.md) — a layered, multi-Block build 170 - [Reconciler reference](../reference/blocks/reconciler.md) — the most non-trivial Block, when you graduate from one source 171 - [`intropy` CLI reference](../reference/cli/index.md) — every command, every flag 172

1	# Working with AI assistants
2	
3	Intropy ships **agent skills** for AI coding assistants like Claude Code. Each skill teaches the assistant one Intropy capability: the conventions, the load-bearing rules, and how to verify a change. Instead of rediscovering the house style every session, the assistant follows the same playbook an Intropy maintainer would.
4	
5	## What Intropy gives an AI assistant
6	
7	An AI assistant is only as good as the structure it works within. A plain .NET repo leaves the big decisions open: which abstraction owns which responsibility, where the wiring goes, what shape a new piece of code should take. An assistant fills those gaps by guessing, and every guess is a chance for the result to drift away from how your team builds. Instead of inventing a design, the assistant works within one and produces accurate, pattern-consistent code.
8	
9	## Enable AI assistance in your project
10	
11	Skills are published as OCI artifacts and managed with the `intropy` CLI.
12	
13	!!! note "Prerequisites"
14	    The [Intropy CLI](../reference/cli/index.md) is on your `PATH` (`intropy --help` prints the verbs), and your AI coding assistant loads `SKILL.md`-format skills. Claude Code is the reference implementation; any assistant that reads the same skill format works.
15	
16	**New integrations get skills at scaffold time.** After rendering a Blueprint, `intropy int create` offers to install the Intropy skill collection into the new project (`[Y/n]`, default yes):
17	
18	```console
19	$ intropy int create hello-world -n OrderSync
20	created OrderSync (blueprint hello-world)
21	Install agent skills into .agents/skills? [Y/n]:
22	  installed intropy-pipeline @ 0.1.1
23	  ... 8 more ...
24	installed 9 skill(s) from harbor.intropy.io/skills/index:latest
25	```
26	
27	In non-interactive runs (CI, the Backstage scaffolder) the prompt is skipped; pass `--install-skills` to install without prompting, or `--skip-install-skills` to opt out silently.
28	
29	Alongside the skills, every scaffolded project carries an `AGENTS.md`: a facts-only project manifest following the [agents.md](https://agents.md/) standard, stating what the component is, its component and topic names, ports, key files, and the canonical run command (`task run` when the project ships a `Taskfile.yml`). Most coding assistants load `AGENTS.md` automatically; for Claude Code, which reads `CLAUDE.md`, the scaffold includes a one-line `CLAUDE.md` that imports it.
30	
31	**Existing projects register the collection once.** This caches the catalogue index so skills can be installed by name:
32	
33	```bash
34	intropy skills collection add --name intropy \
35	  --ref harbor.intropy.io/skills/index:latest
36	intropy skills add --name intropy-getting-started
37	```
38	
39	Either way, skills land in the project's `.agents/skills/` directory, and the CLI records them in two files at the project root: `skills.json` (what's registered and installed) and `skills.lock.json` (exact digests and install paths). Commit both — that's what makes the skill set travel with the repo, so teammates and CI agents that open the project get identical skills. To pin an exact version, install by full OCI reference instead of by name:
40	
41	```bash
42	intropy skills add harbor.intropy.io/skills/intropy-pipeline:0.1.1
43	```
44	
45	When the catalogue publishes a new version, refresh the cached index and reconcile:
46	
47	```bash
48	intropy skills collection update intropy
49	intropy skills update --all
50	```
51	
52	## The skill catalogue
53	
54	The catalogue is deliberately fine-grained: one capability per skill. Each skill's description carries the trigger situations it covers and explicit redirects to its siblings, so the assistant loads exactly the guidance the task needs. Ask it to write a step class and it gets the Block conventions; ask it to wire that step into the pipeline and it gets the composition rules instead. Every skill ends with a verification section, so the assistant doesn't just make the change: it builds, runs, and checks the expected output before reporting done.
55	
56	The full catalogue, including what's planned, lives in the [intropy-skills repository](https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-skills). To see what's already installed in a project, run `intropy skills list`.
57	
58	## Machine-readable docs
59	
60	This documentation site is also exposed in a form built for AI consumption. Point your assistant at:
61	
62	- `https://docs.intropy.example/llms.txt` — a structured index of canonical pages, following the [llmstxt.org](https://llmstxt.org/) convention.
63	
64	The `llms.txt` file is the right input when an assistant needs the docs but shouldn't ingest the full site. It enumerates Concepts, References, How-tos, and Tutorials with one-line descriptions so the assistant can fetch the page that actually answers the question.
65	
66	## What's next
67	
68	- [Quick start](quick-start.md) — scaffold and run your first integration by hand
69	- [Migrate to Intropy with AI assistance](../migration/with-ai-assistance.md) — the AI-assisted migration loop for BizTalk solutions
70	- [`intropy` CLI reference](../reference/cli/index.md) — the commands the skills wrap
